summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.

key_cases.case_name: Mississippi Department of Human Services v. D.C.
key_cases.holding: The Court held that Section 43-15-125 immunizes the Department and its officers from claims arising out of its licensing and licensing-related investigation of a foster home, but affirmed the denial of summary judgment on the foster child's remaining Tort Claims Act allegations about his care.
key_cases.relevance: Licensing of the foster home in which a child is placed is immunized conduct, which shapes what a placement claim can allege.
key_cases.quote: Section 43-15-125 grants immunity to DHS for its licensing of foster homes.

key_cases.holding: Reviewing the statute de novo, the Court reversed a youth court's bypass of reunification, holding that Section 43-21-603(7)(c) requires both one of the three enumerated criteria and a best-interest finding, and that a father's pre-birth criminal history was not conduct to which he subjected the child.
key_cases.relevance: Foster placement without a reunification plan requires findings the youth court here could not make.
key_cases.quote: after determining that one of the first three criteria have been met, the youth court must also determine that bypassing reunification is in the best interests of the child

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed in part the denial of qualified immunity, holding that an unsuitable living situation, without evidence of imminent danger, is not exigency justifying a warrantless removal.
key_cases.relevance: Foster placement entered without exigency or a court order is constitutionally infirm from the outset.
key_cases.quote: Unsuitable as R.B.’s living situation may have been, it did not constitute exigent circumstances necessitating warrantless removal from his mother.

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's grant of durable legal custody of a chronically abused child to her long-time foster parents, but reversed the portion of the judgment permanently relieving the Department of Human Services of any further involvement, holding that durable legal custody leaves the parents' residual rights intact and ends only the mandatory annual dispositional reviews, not the youth court's jurisdiction or the Department's ability to monitor.
key_cases.relevance: A long-term foster placement became the child's permanency outcome without terminating the mother's residual rights or her supervised visitation.
key_cases.quote: The fact that under durable legal custody the parent retains some form of residual rights and responsibilities is a vital and obvious distinction to termination of parental rights.
